en.greeting: Hi! Today we go further with rules: must or have to, rules in the past and future, what you're allowed to do, and what might happen. Let's start!

steps.title: must or have to?
steps.text: Quick recap: **have to / must** = harus, **mustn't** = dilarang, **don't have to** = tidak perlu. Now: which *harus* do you choose?
steps.body:
Indonesian has one word, *harus*. English has a simple guide:
**must** = you feel it's important yourself, or it's a **written rule** (signs, notices, laws): *I must call my grandmother. Visitors must sign in.*
**have to** = the rule comes **from outside**: your boss, your company, a timetable, the situation: *I have to use the VPN at home.*
Often both are fine, and **have to** is the safe choice when you speak.

steps.title: Who made the rule?
steps.text: Dimas works at a bank in Surabaya. He says: 'I have to wear a batik shirt every Friday.'

options: Dimas himself: he loves batik.
His office: it's a company rule.
Nobody: it isn't necessary.
question.explanation: **have to** = the obligation comes from outside: here his office. *I must* is more typical for his own feeling. 'It isn't necessary' would be **don't have to**.

steps.title: Past and future: had to, will have to
steps.text: *Kemarin saya harus lembur.* How do you say that? Careful: **must** has no past and no future form!
steps.body:
Past: **had to** + base verb, the same for every subject. *Yesterday I must work late* is wrong → **Yesterday I had to work late.**
Future: **will have to** ('ll have to) + base verb. Never 'will must'.
Not necessary: **didn't have to** (past), **won't have to** (future).
The verb after had to stays in the base form: *she had to go*, not 'had to went'. Indonesian doesn't change the verb, so look at the time words: *yesterday, last week, tomorrow, next month*.

steps.title: Stuck on the KRL
steps.text: Yesterday the KRL broke down between two stations. Rina tells her boss what happened.

question.prompt: Arrange the words: Kami harus menunggu satu jam.
question.solution: We had to wait for an hour.
question.explanation: Past obligation = **had to** + base verb: **We had to wait** … must has no past form, and *wait* stays in the base form after had to.

steps.title: be allowed to: boleh and tidak boleh
steps.text: To talk about permission (*izin*), use **be allowed to**.
steps.body:
**am / is / are allowed to** + base verb = *boleh, diizinkan*: *We're allowed to work from home on Fridays.*
**am / is / are not allowed to** = *tidak boleh, dilarang*. Past: **was / were (not) allowed to**. Question: **Are we allowed to …?**
The trap: *Kami tidak diizinkan* has no to be, so learners say 'We not allowed' or 'We are not allow'. You need **are**, and **allowed** always ends in **-ed** (like *di-izinkan*: Indonesian adds di-, English adds -ed).

steps.title: Explain the sign
steps.text: There's a sign in your office: **NO SMOKING INSIDE THE BUILDING**. A new colleague asks you about it.

options: Staff are not allow to smoke inside.
Staff don't allowed to smoke inside.
Staff are not allowed to smoke inside.
question.explanation: be + not + **allowed** to: **are not allowed to**. 'not allow' is missing the -ed, and 'don't allowed' uses do instead of are.

steps.title: may, might, could = mungkin
steps.text: When something is possible but you're not sure, English uses **may, might** or **could**.
steps.body:
**may / might / could** + base verb = *mungkin*. **might** is the most common in speaking, **may** is a bit more formal, **could** = it's possible. Negative: **might not / may not** (*mungkin tidak*). No to, no -s.
The trap: *mungkin* is also **maybe**, a separate word at the start: *Maybe I'll come* or *I might come*, not 'I maybe come'.
And don't drop **be**: *Servernya mungkin mati* → *The server **might be** down*.

steps.title: Not answering
steps.text: You call your colleague Sari three times, but she isn't answering her phone.

options: She might be busy.
She maybe busy.
She might busy.
question.explanation: **might + be + busy**: *busy* isn't a verb, so you need **be** after might. *maybe* is a separate word (Maybe she's busy), so 'She maybe busy' is wrong.

steps.title: could and may: other jobs
steps.text: Wait: you learnt **could** and **may** before, with a different meaning! The rule isn't broken: these words have more than one job.
steps.body: **could** = past ability (*dulu bisa*) or a polite request (*Could you …?*). **May I …?** = asking permission. **could / may** about now or the future when you're not sure = *mungkin*. The context tells you which job.

examples.en: When I was young, I could run 5 km.
examples.id: Waktu muda, saya bisa lari 5 km.

examples.en: Could you send me the file, please?
examples.id: Bisa tolong kirim filenya ke saya?

examples.en: Check the address again. The map could be wrong.
examples.id: Cek alamatnya lagi. Petanya bisa saja salah.

examples.en: The shop may be closed on Sunday.

steps.title: Which could is mungkin?
steps.text: Three sentences, three different jobs for **could**.

question.prompt: Which sentence uses could for possibility (mungkin)?
options: When I was a student, I could sleep for ten hours.
Could you close the door, please?
Take a jacket. It could be cold in Bandung tonight.
question.explanation: *It could be cold tonight* = maybe it will be cold, you aren't sure: **possibility**. *When I was a student, I could …* is past ability (dulu bisa), and *Could you …?* is a polite request.

steps.title: Cheat sheet
steps.text: Here's the whole lesson on one page. Keep it for the next time you explain a rule or make a plan!

artifact.title: Cheat sheet · must, have to, allowed, might
artifact.intro: must / have to = necessary. had to = past, will have to = future. be allowed to = permission. may / might / could = possible (mungkin).
rows: Visitors must sign in at reception.
I have to use the VPN at home.
You don't have to come if you're busy.
Yesterday I had to work late.
We didn't have to go to the office.
Next year you'll have to pay for the app.
am / is / are allowed to + verb
We're allowed to work from home on Fridays.
am / is / are not allowed to + verb
Students aren't allowed to use phones in the exam.
I wasn't allowed to stay up late.
I might not come to the party.
tips: **must** = your own feeling or a written rule; **have to** = a rule from outside. Often both are fine: **have to** is safe in speaking.
**must has no past or future**: had to, will have to. Never 'Yesterday I must' or 'will must'.
**allowed** needs -ed and am / is / are. **might** goes before the verb; *maybe* is a separate word at the start.

examples.en: I must call my grandmother this weekend.
examples.id: Saya harus menelepon nenek akhir pekan ini.

examples.en: Are we allowed to bring food into the cinema?
examples.id: Apakah kita boleh bawa makanan ke bioskop?

examples.en: The server may be down. Let me check.
examples.id: Servernya mungkin mati. Saya cek dulu.

steps.title: Watch and read
steps.text: Want more? Watch a short BBC video about have to and must, and read the British Council page on may and might.

id.greeting: Hai! Hari ini kita belajar lebih jauh tentang aturan: must atau have to, aturan di masa lalu dan masa depan, apa yang boleh kamu lakukan, dan apa yang mungkin terjadi. Yuk, mulai!

steps.title: must atau have to?
steps.text: Ulasan singkat: **have to / must** = harus, **mustn't** = dilarang, **don't have to** = tidak perlu. Sekarang: *harus* yang mana yang kamu pilih?
steps.body:
Bahasa Indonesia hanya punya satu kata, *harus*. Bahasa Inggris punya panduan sederhana:
**must** = kamu sendiri merasa itu penting, atau itu **aturan tertulis** (papan tanda, pengumuman, undang-undang): *I must call my grandmother. Visitors must sign in.*
**have to** = aturannya datang **dari luar**: bosmu, kantormu, jadwal, keadaan: *I have to use the VPN at home.*
Sering keduanya benar, dan **have to** pilihan aman saat bicara.

steps.title: Siapa yang membuat aturannya?
steps.text: Dimas bekerja di sebuah bank di Surabaya. Dia berkata: 'I have to wear a batik shirt every Friday.'

options: Dimas himself: he loves batik.
His office: it's a company rule.
Nobody: it isn't necessary.
question.explanation: **have to** = kewajibannya datang dari luar: di sini dari kantornya. Kalau itu perasaannya sendiri, dia lebih mungkin bilang *I must*. 'Tidak perlu' itu **don't have to**.

steps.title: Lampau dan masa depan: had to, will have to
steps.text: *Kemarin saya harus lembur.* Apa bahasa Inggrisnya? Hati-hati: **must** tidak punya bentuk lampau dan masa depan!
steps.body:
Lampau: **had to** + kata kerja dasar, sama untuk semua subjek. *Yesterday I must work late* itu salah → **Yesterday I had to work late.**
Masa depan: **will have to** ('ll have to) + kata kerja dasar. Jangan 'will must'.
Tidak perlu: **didn't have to** (lampau), **won't have to** (nanti).
Kata kerja sesudah had to tetap bentuk dasar: *she had to go*, bukan 'had to went'. Bahasa Indonesia tidak mengubah kata kerja, jadi perhatikan kata waktunya: *yesterday, last week, tomorrow, next month*.

steps.title: Terjebak di KRL
steps.text: Kemarin KRL mogok di antara dua stasiun. Rina menceritakan kejadiannya ke bosnya.

question.prompt: Susun kata-katanya: Kami harus menunggu satu jam.
question.solution: We had to wait for an hour.
question.explanation: Kewajiban di masa lalu = **had to** + kata kerja dasar: **We had to wait** … must tidak punya bentuk lampau, dan *wait* tetap bentuk dasar sesudah had to.

steps.title: be allowed to: boleh dan tidak boleh
steps.text: Untuk membicarakan *izin*, pakai **be allowed to**.
steps.body:
**am / is / are allowed to** + kata kerja dasar = *boleh, diizinkan*: *We're allowed to work from home on Fridays.*
**am / is / are not allowed to** = *tidak boleh, dilarang*. Lampau: **was / were (not) allowed to**. Pertanyaan: **Are we allowed to …?**
Jebakannya: *Kami tidak diizinkan* tidak punya to be, jadi orang sering bilang 'We not allowed' atau 'We are not allow'. Kamu perlu **are**, dan **allowed** selalu berakhiran **-ed** (mirip *di-izinkan*: bahasa Indonesia menambah di-, bahasa Inggris menambah -ed).

steps.title: Jelaskan papannya
steps.text: Ada papan di kantormu: **NO SMOKING INSIDE THE BUILDING**. Rekan kerja baru bertanya tentang papan itu.

options: Staff are not allow to smoke inside.
Staff don't allowed to smoke inside.
Staff are not allowed to smoke inside.
question.explanation: be + not + **allowed** to: **are not allowed to**. 'not allow' kehilangan -ed, dan 'don't allowed' memakai do, padahal seharusnya are.

steps.title: may, might, could = mungkin
steps.text: Kalau sesuatu bisa terjadi tapi kamu tidak yakin, bahasa Inggris memakai **may, might** atau **could**.
steps.body:
**may / might / could** + kata kerja dasar = *mungkin*. **might** paling sering dipakai saat bicara, **may** sedikit lebih formal, **could** = bisa saja terjadi. Negatif: **might not / may not** (*mungkin tidak*). Tanpa to, tanpa -s.
Jebakannya: *mungkin* juga bisa **maybe**, kata terpisah di awal kalimat: *Maybe I'll come* atau *I might come*, bukan 'I maybe come'.
Dan jangan lupa **be**: *Servernya mungkin mati* → *The server **might be** down*.

steps.title: Tidak diangkat
steps.text: Kamu menelepon rekan kerjamu Sari tiga kali, tapi dia tidak mengangkat teleponnya.

options: She might be busy.
She maybe busy.
She might busy.
question.explanation: **might + be + busy**: *busy* bukan kata kerja, jadi perlu **be** sesudah might. *maybe* adalah kata terpisah (Maybe she's busy), jadi 'She maybe busy' salah.

steps.title: could dan may: tugas lain
steps.text: Tunggu: kamu sudah belajar **could** dan **may** sebelumnya, dengan arti lain! Aturannya tidak rusak: kata-kata ini punya lebih dari satu tugas.
steps.body: **could** = kemampuan di masa lalu (*dulu bisa*) atau permintaan sopan (*Could you …?*). **May I …?** = minta izin. **could / may** tentang sekarang atau nanti saat kamu tidak yakin = *mungkin*. Konteksnya yang menunjukkan tugas mana.

examples.en: When I was young, I could run 5 km.
examples.id: Waktu muda, saya bisa lari 5 km.

examples.en: Could you send me the file, please?
examples.id: Bisa tolong kirim filenya ke saya?

examples.en: Check the address again. The map could be wrong.
examples.id: Cek alamatnya lagi. Petanya bisa saja salah.

examples.en: The shop may be closed on Sunday.

steps.title: could yang mana artinya mungkin?
steps.text: Tiga kalimat, tiga tugas berbeda untuk **could**.

question.prompt: Kalimat mana yang memakai could untuk kemungkinan (mungkin)?
options: When I was a student, I could sleep for ten hours.
Could you close the door, please?
Take a jacket. It could be cold in Bandung tonight.
question.explanation: *It could be cold tonight* = mungkin nanti malam dingin, kamu tidak yakin: **kemungkinan**. *When I was a student, I could …* adalah kemampuan di masa lalu (dulu bisa), dan *Could you …?* adalah permintaan sopan.
